{{Short description|Mathematical theorem about the Fourier series}}
In mathematics, '''Fejér's theorem''',<ref>Lipót Fejér, [https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k3087z/f984.item.r= « Sur les fonctions intégrables et bornées »], ''[[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences|C.R. Acad. Sci. Paris]]'', 10 décembre 1900, 984-987, .</ref><ref>Leopold Fejér, [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=inu.30000106096518&view=1up&seq=61 Untersuchungen über Fouriersche Reihen], ''[[Mathematische Annalen]]'', [https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN235181684_0058 vol. 58], 1904, 51-69.</ref> named after [[Hungary|Hungarian]] [[mathematician]] [[Lipót Fejér]], states the following:<ref name=":0">{{Citation |title=Introduction |date=1988-07-21 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139172011.002 |work=An Introduction to Hilbert Space |pages=1–3 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |access-date=2022-11-14}}</ref>

{{math_theorem
| math_statement = Let  <math> f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C} </math> be a continuous function with period <math>2\pi</math>, let <math>s_n(f)</math> be the <math>n</math>th [[partial sum]] of the [[Fourier series]] of <math>f</math>, and let <math>\sigma_n(f)</math> be the sequence of [[Cesàro means]] of the sequence <math> s_n(f)</math>, that is the sequence of [[arithmetic means]] of <math>s_0(f), \ldots, s_n(f)</math>. Then the sequence <math>\sigma_n(f)</math> [[Uniform convergence|converges uniformly]] to <math>f </math> on <math> \mathbb{R} </math> as n tends to infinity.
| name = Fejér's Theorem
}}

== Explanation of Fejér's Theorem's ==
Explicitly, we can write the Fourier series of <math>f</math> as

<math display="block">f(x)= \sum_{n=- \infty}^{\infty} c_n \, e^{inx}</math>

where the <math>n</math>th partial sum of the Fourier series of <math>f</math> may be written as
:<math>s_n(f,x)=\sum_{k=-n}^nc_ke^{ikx},</math>
where the Fourier coefficients <math>c_k</math> are
:<math>c_k=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(t)e^{-ikt}dt.</math>
Then, we can define
:<math>\sigma_n(f,x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}s_k(f,x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x-t)F_n(t)dt </math>
with <math>F_n</math> being the <math>n</math>th order [[Fejér kernel]].
Then, Fejér's theorem asserts that

<math display="block">\lim_{n\to \infty} \sigma_n (f, x) = f(x)</math>

with uniform convergence. With the convergence written out explicitly, the above statement becomes

<math display="block">\forall \epsilon > 0 \, \exist\, n_0 \in \mathbb{N}:  n \geq n_0 \implies | f(x) - \sigma_n(f,x)| < \epsilon, \, \forall x \in  \mathbb{R}</math>

== Proof of Fejér's Theorem ==
We first prove the following lemma:

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = The <math>n</math>th partial sum of the Fourier series <math>s_n(f,x)</math> may be written using the Dirichlet Kernel as
:<math> s_n(f,x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x-t) \, D_n(t) \, dt </math>
| name = Lemma 1
}}

<u>Proof</u>: Recall the definition of <math>D_n(x)</math>, the [[Dirichlet kernel|Dirichlet Kernel]]:

<math display="block">D_n(x) = \sum_{k=-n}^n e^{ikx}</math>. 

We substitute the integral form of the Fourier coefficients into the formula for <math>s_n(f,x)</math> above

<math display="block">s_n(f,x)=\sum_{k=-n}^n c_ke^{ikx} = \sum_{k=-n}^n [\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(t)e^{-ikt}dt ] e^{ikx} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(t) \sum_{k=-n}^n e^{ik(x-t)} \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(t) \, D_n(x-t) \, dt.</math>

Using a change of variables we get

<math display="block">s_n(f,x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x-t) \, D_n(t) \, dt.</math>

This completes the proof of Lemma 1.

We next prove the following lemma:

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = The nth Cesaro sum <math> \sigma_n(f,x) </math> may be written using the Fejér Kernel as: <math> \sigma_n(f,x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x-t)F_n(t)dt </math>
| name = Lemma 2
}}

<u>Proof</u>: Recall the definition of the [[Fejér kernel|Fejér Kernel]] <math>F_n(x)</math>

<math display="block">F_n(x)  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}D_k(x)</math>

As in the case of Lemma 1, we substitute the integral form of the Fourier coefficients into the formula for <math>\sigma_n(f,x)</math>

<math display="block">\sigma_n(f,x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}s_k(f,x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x-t) \, D_k(t) \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  f(x-t) \, [\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} D_k(t)] \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  f(x-t) \, F_n(t) \, dt</math>

This completes the proof of Lemma 2.

We next prove the 3rd Lemma:

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = The Fejer Kernel has the following 3 properties:
* a) <math> \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi F_n (x) \, dx =1</math>
* b) <math> F_n(x) \geq 0 </math>
* c) For all fixed <math> \delta > 0 </math>, <math> \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{\delta \leq |x| \leq \pi} F_n (x) \, dx = 0 </math>
| name = Lemma 3
}}

<u>Proof</u>: a) Given that <math>F_n</math> is the mean of <math>D_n</math>, the integral of which is 1, by linearity, the integral of <math>F_n</math> is also equal to 1.

b) As <math>D_n(x)</math> is a geometric sum, we get a simple formula for <math>D_n(x)</math> and then for <math>F_n(x)</math>, using [[De Moivre's formula]]:

<math display="block">F_n(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\sin((2k + 1) x / 2)}{\sin(x / 2)} = \frac{1}{n} \frac{\sin^2(n x / 2)}{\sin^2(x / 2)} \geq 0</math>

c) For all fixed <math>\delta > 0</math>,

<math display="block">\int_{\delta \leq |x| \leq \pi} F_n (x) \, dx = \frac{2}{n} \int_{\delta \leq x \leq \pi} \frac{\sin^2(n x / 2)}{\sin^2(x / 2)} \, dx \leq \frac{2}{n} \int_{\delta \leq x \leq \pi} \frac{1}{\sin^2(x / 2)} \, dx</math>

This shows that the integral converges to zero, as <math>n</math> goes to infinity.
This completes the proof of Lemma 3.

We are now ready to prove Fejér's Theorem. First, let us recall the statement we are trying to prove

<math display="block">\forall \epsilon > 0 \, \exist\, n_0 \in \mathbb{N}:  n \geq n_0 \implies | f(x) - \sigma_n(f,x)| < \epsilon, \, \forall x \in  \mathbb{R}</math>

We want to find an expression for <math>|\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |</math>. We begin by invoking Lemma 2:

<math display="block">\sigma_n(f,x)= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  f(x-t) \, F_n(t) \, dt.</math>

By Lemma 3a we know that

<math display="block">\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  f(x-t) \, F_n(t) \, dt - f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  f(x-t) \, F_n(t) \, dt - f(x) \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi F_n(t) \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  f(x-t) \, F_n(t) \, dt - \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x) \, F_n(t) \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  [f(x-t)-f(x)] \, F_n(t) \, dt. </math>

Applying the [[triangle inequality]] yields

<math display="block">|\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |= |\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  [f(x-t)-f(x)] \, F_n(t) \, dt| \leq \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  |[f(x-t)-f(x)] \, F_n(t)| \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  |f(x-t)-f(x)| \, |F_n(t)| \, dt, </math>

and by Lemma 3b, we get

<math display="block">|\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |=  \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi  |f(x-t)-f(x)| \, F_n(t) \, dt. </math>

We now split the integral into two parts, integrating over the two regions <math>|t| \leq \delta</math> and <math> \delta \leq |t| \leq \pi</math>.

<math display="block">|\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |=  \left( \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{|t| \leq \delta}  |f(x-t)-f(x)| \, F_n(t) \, dt \right) +  \left( \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\delta \leq|t|\leq \pi}  |f(x-t)-f(x)| \, F_n(t) \, dt \right)  </math>

The motivation for doing so is that we want to prove that <math>\lim_{n \to \infty} |\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |=0</math>. We can do this by proving that each integral above, integral 1 and integral 2, goes to zero. This is precisely what we will do in the next step.

We first note that the function <math>f</math> is continuous on <math>[-\pi,\pi]</math>. We invoke [[Heine–Cantor theorem|the theorem]] that every [[periodic function]] on <math>[-\pi,\pi]</math> that is continuous is also bounded and uniformily continuous. This means that 
:<math>\forall \epsilon > 0,\exist \delta > 0: |x-y| \leq \delta \implies |f(x)-f(y)| \leq \epsilon</math>. 
Hence we can rewrite the integral 1 as follows

<math display="block">\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{|t| \leq \delta}  |f(x-t)-f(x)| \, F_n(t) \, dt \leq \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{|t| \leq \delta}  \epsilon \, F_n(t) \, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon \int_{|t| \leq \delta}  \, F_n(t) \, dt </math>

Because <math>F_n(x) \geq 0, \forall x\in \mathbb{R}</math> and <math>\delta \leq \pi</math>

<math display="block">\frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon \int_{|t| \leq \delta}  \, F_n(t) \, dt \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon \int_{-\pi}^\pi  \, F_n(t) \, dt  </math>

By Lemma 3a we then get for all n

<math display="block">\frac{1}{2\pi}\epsilon \int_{-\pi}^\pi  \, F_n(t) \, dt = \epsilon </math>

This gives the desired bound for integral 1 which we can exploit in final step.

For integral 2, we note that since <math>f</math> is bounded, we can write this bound as <math>M=\sup_{-\pi \leq t \leq \pi} |f(t)|</math>

<math display="block"> \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\delta \leq|t|\leq \pi}  |f(x-t)-f(x)| \, F_n(t) \, dt \leq \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\delta \leq|t|\leq \pi} 2M \, F_n(t) \, dt
= \frac{M}{\pi} \int_{\delta \leq|t|\leq \pi}F_n(t) \, dt </math>

We are now ready to prove that <math>\lim_{n \to \infty} |\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |=0</math>. We begin by writing

<math display="block">|\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) | \leq \epsilon \, + \frac{M}{\pi} \int_{\delta \leq|t|\leq \pi}F_n(t) \, dt </math>

Thus,

<math display="block">\lim_{n \to \infty} |\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |\leq \lim_{n \to \infty} \epsilon \, + \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{M}{\pi} \int_{\delta \leq|t|\leq \pi}F_n(t) \, dt </math>

By Lemma 3c we know that the integral goes to 0 as <math>n</math> goes to infinity, and because epsilon is arbitrary, we can set it equal to 0. Hence <math>\lim_{n \to \infty} |\sigma_n(f,x) - f(x) |=0</math>, which completes the proof.

== Modifications and Generalisations of Fejér's Theorem ==
In fact, Fejér's theorem can be modified to hold for [[pointwise convergence]].<ref name=":0" />

{{math_theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>f \in L^2(- \pi, \pi)</math> be continuous at <math>x\in(-\pi,\pi)</math>, then <math>\sigma_n(f,x)</math> converges pointwise as n goes to infinity.
| name = Modified Fejér's Theorem
}}

Sadly however, the theorem does not work in a general sense when we replace the sequence <math>\sigma_n (f,x)</math> with <math>s_n (f,x)</math>. This is because there exist functions whose Fourier series fails to converge at some point.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Rogosinski |first=W. W. |last2=Rogosinski |first2=H. P. |date=December 1965 |title=An elementary companion to a theorem of J. Mercer |journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]] |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=311–322 |doi=10.1007/bf02806398 | doi-access= |issn=0021-7670}}</ref> However, the set of points at which a function in <math>L^2(-\pi, \pi)</math> diverges has to be measure zero. This fact, called Lusins conjecture or [[Carleson's theorem]], was proved in 1966 by [[Lennart Carleson|L. Carleson]].<ref name=":1" /> We can however prove a corollary relating which goes as follows:

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math> s_n \in \mathbb{C}, \, \forall n \in \, \mathbb{Z}_+ </math>. If  <math>s_n </math> converges to <math>s</math> as <math>n</math> goes to infinity, then <math>\sigma_n</math> converges to <math>s</math> as <math>n</math> goes to infinity.
| name = Corollary
}}

A more general form of the theorem applies to functions which are not necessarily continuous {{harv|Zygmund|1968|loc=Theorem III.3.4}}. Suppose that <math>f</math> is in <math>L^1(-\pi,\pi)</math>. If the left and right limits <math>f(x_0\pm 0)</math> of <math>f(x)</math> exist at <math>x_0</math>, or if both limits are infinite of the same sign, then

:<math>\sigma_n(x_0) \to \frac{1}{2}\left(f(x_0+0)+f(x_0-0)\right).</math>

Existence or divergence to infinity of the Cesàro mean is also implied. By a theorem of [[Marcel Riesz]], Fejér's theorem holds precisely as stated if the (C, 1) mean <math>\sigma_n</math> is replaced with [[Cesàro summation|(C, &alpha;) mean]] of the Fourier series {{harv|Zygmund|1968|loc=Theorem III.5.1}}.
